name: Johann Sebastian Bach
title: Johann Sebastian Bach: craft, Scripture, and music for the congregation
description: The work of a church musician whose music was born among rehearsals, teaching, and the readings of the Christian calendar.

sections.heading: Learning a craft among musicians
paragraphs: Johann Sebastian Bach was born in Eisenach in 1685, into a family of musicians. He lost his parents as a child and went to live with his brother Johann Christoph, an organist in Ohrdruf. There he continued his education, sang in the school choir, and learned to play the organ.

His career included posts in Arnstadt, Mühlhausen, Weimar, and Köthen before he arrived in Leipzig. The Bach-Archiv timeline shows years of learning, professional responsibilities, and changes of employment. The music we hear today was tied to specific instruments, institutions, and the people who performed it.

sections.heading: Everyday service in Leipzig
paragraphs: In 1723 he took up the post of cantor of St. Thomas in Leipzig. His duties included teaching and preparing music for worship. The cantatas brought together Bible texts, religious poetry, and congregational singing within the city’s Lutheran setting; producing them required both composing and working with the performers.

He remained in Leipzig until his death in 1750. His sacred works include the St. John Passion and the St. Matthew Passion. His legacy also includes instrumental music and other genres: recognizing the Christian dimension of his work does not require erasing the breadth of his musical activity.

reflection: Colossians 3:16 connects the word of Christ with teaching, admonishing, and singing with gratitude. Music can help a community remember and meditate, as long as its content is understood and examined. The beauty of sound invites us to listen; discernment also pays attention to the words being sung.

Behind a song there is preparation: choosing a text, rehearsing, listening to the group, and adjusting how each one takes part. We do not need to measure every act of service against Bach’s fame. We can take care of the craft we have received and seek to have our music support the faith of those who gather, without making the performer the center.
review_note: We avoid attributing popular sayings to the composer without documentary support. The Lutheran context of his music is distinguished from Verbo’s editorial reflection; his personal life is not idealized.
source_labels: Bach-Archiv Leipzig. “Johann Sebastian Bach – A chronology.”
